builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted model uses more compute or memory than your workload can justify.
builder_plan.change: Check for a usable pruned checkpoint and runtime support before attempting model surgery.
builder_plan.baseline: The original unpruned model at the same precision, context, and load.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task quality, actual GPU memory, serving throughput, and preparation cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Fewer Heads, Fewer Memories: Pruning Redundant Attention Heads Suppresses Verbatim Memorisation
summary: The method replaces retraining-based or data-modification-based memorisation mitigation with a one-time identification and zeroing of task-redundant attention heads before inference. It costs an offline redundancy-identification pass over a benchmark and adds no runtime memory or latency overhead, since zeroed heads can be fused or skipped, though the paper evaluates only perplexity as the quality proxy. It can fail when memorisation is distributed across heads not flagged as redundant, when the identification benchmark mismatches the production workload, or when tasks depend on the pruned heads despite aggregate perplexity appearing stable.
rationale: Head pruning is cheap to implement on a 24 GB GPU and the privacy benefit is substantial, but the evidence is limited to GPT-2-XL and perplexity, so workload-specific validation of both memorisation suppression and task quality is required before production adoption.
technique: Inference-time attention-head pruning for memorisation suppression

claims.statement: The method replaces retraining-based or data-modification-based memorisation mitigation with a one-time identification and zeroing of task-redundant attention heads before inference. It costs an offline redundancy-identification pass over a benchmark and adds no runtime memory or latency overhead, since zeroed heads can be fused or skipped, though the paper evaluates only perplexity as the quality proxy. It can fail when memorisation is distributed across heads not flagged as redundant, when the identification benchmark mismatches the production workload, or when tasks depend on the pruned heads despite aggregate perplexity appearing stable.

Pruning 729 task-redundant attention heads in GPT-2-XL (1.5B) reduces verbatim memorisation count by 91.5% while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92 (an absolute point change, not a multiplicative factor).
